seasons.review_body: Aashram launched on MX Player on August 28, 2020 - notable as a free-to-stream original at a time when Indian OTT was still largely paywalled. Prakash Jha directed Bobby Deol as Baba Nirala, a self-appointed spiritual leader whose ashram operates as a political patronage machine and a cover for exploitation. NDTV rated it 3 out of 5 stars, praising Jha's ambition and Deol's commitment to the role while noting the series' structural flaws: an episode count that invites padding, and self-censorship that softens the edges of the critique the premise requires. The 6.6 IMDb aggregate across the series reflects audiences registering the gap between a compelling central performance and uneven craft around it. Deol's career rehabilitation angle - this was a genuine second act after years of decline - became inseparable from the show's reception narrative.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Aashram S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Pammi** knows how to fight before the system knows what to do with her. She says attack first, defend later, and for a moment the episode moves with that clean sporting logic. Then the ruling lands, the match slips away, and the hour begins its real work: showing how quickly a personal injustice becomes a community wound. By the time **Babaji** is asked to withdraw an FIR and free doctors, the boxing ring has expanded into a street, a hospital, and a crowd waiting for instruction. The premiere works best when it treats authority as choreography.

## Pammi Throws the First Punch, Then the System Throws Back

The opening stretch gives **Johnny** a useful spark. He refuses to name Pammi and clashes with **Nikhil**, framing loyalty as action rather than sentiment. Soon after, Johnny wakes Pammi's area, and Babaji's urgency enters before Babaji fully takes over the frame. That matters. The premiere opens with people being moved, summoned, pressured.

Pammi's boxing beat is the cleanest writing in the episode because it has a simple rule: attack first, then defend. That strategy gives her a sporting identity before the larger machinery crowds in. The "Bravo" she earns confirms that her instinct has discipline behind it.

Then the disqualification arrives, and the judge's ruling is contested as favoritism. The hour's thesis snaps into place. Aashram cares less about whether Pammi can fight than about who decides when her fight counts. Her anger is specific. The match outcome matters, along with the insult of process. When **Mr. Singh** promises to sort things out and suggests appeals, he offers rules as a pressure valve. The episode is already asking whether procedure can cool a wound that everyone can see bleeding.

## The Ring Becomes a Procession

The procession fight widens the lens, and the move works because it grows from the same grievance. The unfairness that bruises Pammi's match now travels into the street. **Satti's** side attacks, **Noni** is involved, and the conflict turns from competitive grievance into public damage.

This is where the pacing starts to show its seams. The dossier's tone notes point to long cut-point silences before abrupt shifts, and the structure bears that out. Explanatory scenes give way to confrontations with little cushioning. Sometimes the sharpness helps. The jump from contained anger to street violence gives the hour a jagged pulse. At other points, the drama feels assembled in hard blocks instead of escalating through pressure.

Still, the choice to move from ring to procession is strong. A weaker premiere would keep Pammi's disqualification as a sports setback. This one uses it as proof of a larger social design. Personal defeat becomes communal exposure. The show understands that rules do not fail quietly here. When they fail, bodies gather around the failure.

## Babaji Enters as the Man Who Stops the Noise

Babaji's function in the episode is fascinating because the writing gives him clashing duties. He wants injured children treated and justice enforced. He stops conflict. He demands treatment. Later, he directs the FIR withdrawal. He wants peace, and his method is command.

That gives the premiere its most valuable tension. Babaji's authority is framed as useful because it cuts through chaos. Doctors must be freed. Treatment must happen. A crowd has to stop interfering. The same authority that calms the situation also decides which legal action should continue and which should disappear. The episode leaves the danger inside the action.

The hospital and FIR material works because it turns morality into procedure. Someone must be treated. Someone must be blamed. Someone must sign, withdraw, comply. Pammi wants the FIR to protect her people from further harm, and she insists on attempt to murder as the legal frame. Later, under Babaji's pressure, she moves toward withdrawal. That pivot is the premiere's sharpest character beat for her. She enters as someone who trusts attack, then learns that the most powerful attack in the room may belong to someone else.

## A Journalist Gets Pushed Out of the Frame

The journalist threatening the mic operator, then being told to get out, is a brief beat with texture. It shows the episode's interest in who controls sound, testimony, and public attention. The mic is not a prop. It is access. Whoever holds it can shape the story around the fight, the injury, and Babaji's intervention.

This beat also exposes one of the premiere's limitations. The hour has plenty of conflict engines: Pammi's match, the procession clash, legal pressure, medical urgency, Babaji's control, media friction. That density gives the episode momentum, but some turns feel announced rather than dramatized. The journalist scene has the force of a signal. It tells the episode's world that public narrative will matter, without giving that conflict enough room to combust.

Even so, the placement is smart. By the time Babaji is asked to withdraw the FIR and free doctors, the episode has already shown that every institution around the injury has its own performance. Sport has judges. Politics has orders. Media has microphones. Faith has crowds. The premiere arranges those performances around one question: who gets obeyed when everyone claims to be solving the same crisis?

## Silence as Control, Silence as Cut

The tone notes mention long silences at key cut-points, and those pauses shape how the episode breathes. The first stretch moves from Pammi's strategy into a silence, then toward the disqualification and its aftermath. Later pauses sit before authority confrontations. Near the end, another extended quiet arrives before procedural resolution.

Those silences are not always elegant. A few transitions pull attention toward the edit rather than the emotion. But the approach fits the hour's subject. Silence in this premiere means waiting. Waiting for a ruling. Waiting for an appeal. Waiting for treatment. Waiting for Babaji's order to be accepted.

That is why the final procedural payoff carries weight even when the writing hurries toward it. The FIR withdrawal does not play like a clean solution. It plays like a test of power. When the legal route Pammi wanted begins to bend under Babaji's direction, the episode leaves the right unease behind. Safety may come from surrendering control. The premiere lets that bargain sit in the room.

## The Verdict

Aashram S1E1 is a solid, loaded premiere with a clear dramatic spine: Pammi fights by rule, then discovers that rules answer to larger forms of authority. The episode's strongest material comes from that escalation, moving from boxing decision to street violence to medical and legal control without losing the thread of who is being pressured. The weakness is shape. Some transitions are too abrupt, and the journalist beat feels more like a planted marker than a fully worked scene. Still, Babaji's contradiction gives the hour bite. He calms the chaos by commanding it, and the episode understands how unsettling that is. As a season opener, it plants Pammi's uncertain path, the unresolved safety question around the FIR, and Babaji's power as the story's central force.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes Baba Nirala's operation in full: the stagecraft of the darbar, the devotees who surrender judgment along with money, and the political functionaries who need him as much as he needs them. Deol is immediately more present than his career at this point suggested he could be.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Nirala's first public appearance as a spiritual figure - the gap between the performer and the performance.

verdict.one_liner: A sturdy premiere turns Pammi's disqualification into a sharper study of who controls justice when crowds gather.

bollymeter.basis: The rapid same-year follow-up raised questions about pacing discipline; the story threads begun in Season 1 continue without significant escalation, and the episode count again tests patience, though the central conspiracy deepens.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 followed Season 1 by less than three months, arriving on November 11, 2020, which raised structural concerns immediately: the production's ambition to keep audiences engaged came at the cost of the careful plotting that the premise required. The nine-episode run continues the investigation threads from Season 1 and deepens the political patronage network around the ashram. The most effective sections are those that focus on the women within the ashram's orbit, particularly Aaditi Pohankar's arc. The show's free-to-stream model on MX Player meant the audience was enormous by Indian OTT standards, but critical coverage was sparser for Season 2 than for the debut season.
seasons.season_over_season: Rapid same-year release; extends Season 1's threads without escalating them - a bridge season rather than a step forward.

bollymeter.basis: The fifteen-episode Season 3 (split across Part 1 in June 2022 and Part 2 in February 2025) is the series' most stretched run; individual episode IMDb ratings in the 6.1 range signal audience fatigue with a story whose central thesis has been stated and re-stated across 33 total episodes.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 arrived in two parts: the first ten episodes on June 3, 2022, and five additional episodes on February 28, 2025. The fifteen-episode total makes Season 3 the largest and most structurally diffuse season. The Ormax Media tracking noted it as a top-watched streaming original across multiple weeks, confirming that the free-to-stream audience for Aashram remains substantial even as critical enthusiasm has not returned to the Season 1 baseline. IMDb episode ratings for Season 3 drop into the low 6s, consistent with a show that has exhausted its central argument without finding a structural way to conclude it. The Part 2 delay of nearly three years further fractured narrative momentum. For viewers committed to the full arc, this is the completion of a long story; for new viewers, it is the least recommended entry point.
seasons.season_over_season: A fifteen-episode run split across three years; biggest audience by platform metrics, lowest episode-level ratings of the entire run.
